parts.text:
38 In a television programme to illustrate scientific models, a presenter fires a gun many times at
a bale of hay. Two small cannon balls are embedded within the hay some distance apart from
each other.
The hay bale measures approximately 2 m × 2 m × 2 m and the cannon balls are made of iron,
approximately spherical, and about 5 cm in diameter.
What might the presenter be illustrating?
A
α-particle scattering
B
β– decay
C
conservation of momentum
D
double-slit interference

hints: Notice the size contrast in the question: a $2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m} \times 2\text{ m}$ bale of hay containing only two $5\text{ cm}$ iron spheres - most of the volume is empty.
Connect that empty volume to the Rutherford model where the atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense nucleus at the centre.
Think of firing many times with a gun as firing many alpha particles at thin gold foil, where most pass straight through and only very few are deflected by a direct hit on a nucleus.
walkthrough: Identify the model parts: the gun firing many times provides many small projectiles, the large $2\text{ m}$ hay bale is a mostly low-density target, and the two $5\text{ cm}$ iron balls are small dense objects hidden inside.

Recall the Rutherford alpha-scattering rule: most $\alpha$-particles pass through gold foil with little deviation because the atom is mostly empty, while a very small fraction come close to a tiny positively charged nucleus and are scattered through large angles.
Map the scales: bullets passing easily through hay models $\alpha$-particles passing through empty atomic space, and rare collisions with the iron balls models rare close encounters with nuclei.

Check the numbers: the balls occupy only a tiny fraction of the bale volume, so most shots will embed in hay undeflected and only a few will hit iron, matching the observed mostly-transmitted with rare-scattered pattern.

Rule out the others: $\beta^-$ decay involves emission from a nucleus, conservation of momentum involves tracking $p = mv$ before and after, and double-slit interference involves wave superposition, none of which use hidden dense targets in a diffuse medium.
The hay-and-cannon-ball demonstration therefore reproduces the logic of the Rutherford experiment. This is option A

A.explanation: Bullets mostly passing through hay with rare hits on the small iron balls models alpha particles mostly passing through empty atoms with rare scattering by tiny nuclei.

B.explanation: Beta-minus decay is a neutron changing to a proton and electron inside one nucleus, not projectiles fired from outside hitting embedded objects.

C.explanation: Conservation of momentum needs measured velocities before and after a collision, not many bullets lost inside a $2\text{ m}$ hay bale.

D.explanation: Double-slit interference needs coherent waves passing through two gaps to form fringes, not bullets stopping in hay or hitting $5\text{ cm}$ spheres.
